title: The body of Christ is created flesh of the uncreated Word
english: If anyone says that the body of Christ is uncreated, and does not confess that he himself — the uncreated God, the Word — showed the incarnation from created humanity and was made man, as it is written, let him be anathema.

How can a body be called uncreated? What is uncreated is also without passion: it cannot be wounded, and it cannot be handled. But Christ, rising from the dead, showed his disciples the marks of the nails and the wound the spear had made, and a body that could be touched, even while he came in when the doors were shut (John 20:19-27). He did this so that the working of the Godhead and the truth of the body might be shown together.
And while he was God, he was recognized as man in the ordinary way; and while he was truly man, he was still shown as God by his works.
notes_covered: Cap. I anathema against calling Christ's body uncreated
Explication: uncreated = impassible/intangible vs risen body handled behind shut doors
Tip scope: Capita I-II only; remaining ten anathemas later

added_allusions.reason: risen body handled; shut doors; nails and spear

translator_notes: Locked from Vossius 1684 Latin column; Greek column OCR too damaged to serve as copy-text.
ANF 6 Crombie exists and was used only as a sense check, not as the reading English.
OCR joins on clavorum/lancea/palpandum disclosed; sense checked against the facing column and the John 20 scene.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Duodecim Capita de Fide, Cap. I (anathema + interpretatio)

title: The flesh is not consubstantial with the Godhead
english: If anyone says that the flesh of Christ is consubstantial with the Godhead, and does not confess that he himself, being in the form of God and God before the ages, emptied himself and took the form of a servant, as it is written (Philippians 2:6-7), let him be anathema.

How can flesh that comes after time be called of the same substance with the everlasting Godhead? That is called consubstantial which is the same in nature, and the same in everlasting duration without change.
notes_covered: Cap. II anathema against homoousion of flesh with divinity
Explication: post-temporal flesh cannot share the Godhead's everlasting sameness

added_allusions.reason: in the form of God; emptied himself; form of a servant

translator_notes: Homoousion kept as the Latin column's Greek loanword, then glossed consubstantial.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Duodecim Capita de Fide, Cap. II (anathema + interpretatio)
